cards.back: The value a digit has because of where it is in a number.
One of the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers.
A number with a decimal point that shows parts of a whole.
The first place to the right of the decimal point, worth 1/10 of a whole.
The second place to the right of the decimal point, worth 1/100 of a whole.
The third place to the right of the decimal point, worth 1/1000 of a whole.
A small raised number that tells how many times to use the base as a factor.
A number like 10, 100, 1,000 made by multiplying 10s.
A number written as the sum of the values of its digits.
A number written in words.
A number written with digits.
Change a number to a nearby number that is easier to use.

cards.front: A digit moves one place to the LEFT. What happens to its value?
cards.back: It becomes 10 times as much.

cards.front: A digit moves one place to the RIGHT. What happens to its value?
cards.back: It becomes 1/10 as much.
450 (each digit moves 2 places left)
0.5, because 5 tenths is more than 4 tenths.
Yes. 3 tenths = 30 hundredths. A zero at the end does not change the value.

cards.front: What do the symbols < and > mean?
cards.back: < means “is less than.” > means “is greater than.” The open side faces the greater number.
6.5 (the hundredths digit is 5, so round up)

cards.front: Why is 0.7 not the same as 0.07?
cards.back: 0.7 is 7 tenths; 0.07 is 7 hundredths, which is 10 times smaller.

cards.front: What number do the blocks show? A flat is 1 whole.
